We provide a taxonomy of current approaches based on their prompting mechanisms and core architectures, and we highlight how these innovations can enhance road scene understanding for autonomous driving, traffic monitoring, and infrastructure maintenance. Finally, we identify key challenges, including real-time performance and safety-critical reliability, and outline a perspective centered on explainable, human-centric AI as a prerequisite for the successful deployment of this technology in next-generation transportation systems.

title: Domain Adaptive LiDAR Panoptic Segmentation via Pseudo-Supervised Instance Learning
authors: Hung Viet Vuong, Myungsik Yoo
abstract: LiDAR panoptic segmentation is a critical task in autonomous driving and robotics, as it combines semantic and instance segmentation to provide a holistic understanding of the environment. A major challenge lies in enabling models to leverage labeled data from one LiDAR sensor while adapting to unlabeled data from a different sensor. This problem, known as domain adaptation, allows models to generalize across varying sensor configurations without requiring additional manual annotations. Although domain adaptation has been widely studied in semantic segmentation, its application to the more complex task of panoptic segmentation remains limited. Existing approaches, such as global feature alignment, aim to match overall feature distributions between source and target domains but fail to capture details at the point and instance level. To address this limitation, we propose Pseudo-supervised Instance Learning for LiDAR Adaptation (PILLA), a framework that trains on both labeled source-domain data and unlabeled target-domain data. PILLA leverages unsupervised clustering to generate pseudo instance labels in the target domain, providing explicit instance-level supervision, which is further reinforced by a dedicated loss function to mitigate the impact of noisy labels. Experiments on the nuScenes dataset show that PILLA outperforms the only prior method, AdaptLPS, by 10.97 percentage points in panoptic quality (PQ), demonstrating the effectiveness of instance-centric domain adaptation.

title: Leveraging Vehicle-Side Detectors With Graph Priors for Roadside Domain Adaptive 3-D Object Detection
authors: Wei Gong, Bowen Wang, Yafei Wang, Chin Long Ng, Jiaming Sun
abstract: The deployment of LiDAR-based 3D roadside measurements and detections in new scenarios involves a labor-intensive process of data collection and annotation. With the rapid development of the high-quality labeled vehicle-side autonomous driving dataset in last few years, it has potential to directly transfer the knowledge and enhance the robustness of roadside LiDAR-based 3D perception model. However, since the domain gaps between different perspectives, it is still suffering a performance degradation when directly applying the training model to unknown roadside scenarios. To this end, we propose a graph-aware self-supervised domain adaptation (GA-RP3D) method to enhance the roadside 3D perception using vehicle-side 3D object detection models. Firstly, we develop a graph-aware knowledge distillation framework to bridge the domain gap, where the learnable regions of interest (ROIs) with spatiotemporal motion states are used to construct global graph nodes and edges. In the adaptive fine-tuning stage, a decoupled graph consistency alignment loss function with a robust kernel is designed to enhance the quality of graph consistency representation and improve training stability. On popular 3D roadside benchmarks and self-collected roadside data, the proposed method demonstrates significant competitiveness compared with the state-of-the-art in the evaluated settings.

title: M3 Detection: Multi-Frame Multi-Level Feature Fusion for Multi-Modal 3-D Object Detection With Camera and 4-D Imaging Radar
authors: Xiaozhi Li, Huijun Di, Jian Li, Feng Liu, Wei Liang
abstract: Recent advances in 4D imaging radar have enabled robust perception in adverse weather, while camera sensors provide dense semantic information. Fusing these complementary modalities has great potential for accurate and cost-effective 3D perception. However, most existing camera-radar fusion methods are limited to single-frame inputs, capturing only a partial view of the scene. The incomplete scene information, compounded by image degradation and 4D radar sparsity, hinders overall detection performance. In contrast, multi-frame fusion offers richer spatial-temporal information but faces two challenges: achieving robust and effective object feature fusion across frames and modalities, and mitigating the computational cost of redundant feature extraction. Consequently, we propose M3Detection, a unified multi-frame 3D object detection framework that performs multi-level feature fusion on multi-modal data from camera and 4D imaging radar. In contrast to conventional architectures, our framework leverages intermediate features from the baseline detector and employs the tracker to produce reference trajectories, improving computational efficiency and providing richer information for second-stage. In the second stage, to address tracking uncertainties and enable fine-grained modeling, we design a global-level inter-object feature aggregation module (GOA) guided by radar information to align global features across candidate proposals and a local-level inter-grid feature aggregation module (LGA) that expands local features along the reference trajectories to enhance fine-grained object representation. The aggregated features are then processed by a trajectory-level multi-frame spatial-temporal fusion module (MSTF) to encode cross-frame interactions and enhance temporal representation. Extensive experiments on the View-of-Delft, TJ4DRadSet, and OmniHD-Scenes datasets demonstrate that M3Detection achieves state-of-the-art 3D detection performance, validating its effectiveness in multi-frame detection with camera-4D imaging radar fusion.

title: Learning Fine-Grained Urban Mobility Dynamics Through Large Model-Enhanced Multimodal Representations
authors: Tianhong Zhao, Jianbin Li, Jinzhou Cao, Wei Tu, Filip Biljecki, Shengao Yi, Zhilu Yuan
abstract: Accurately predicting fine-grained urban mobility is essential for optimizing transportation, accessibility, and urban management. However, existing approaches often depend on dynamic data such as trajectories or signaling records, which are sparsely available across cities, thereby limiting their applicability and generalizability to new urban contexts. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Large Model Enhanced Multimodal Representations (LMEMR) framework to learn hourly grid-level mobility dynamics solely from static geospatial data—including remote sensing imagery, building data, street view imagery, and points of interest—which are widely accessible. Large vision–language models are employed to generate natural-language descriptions of each modality, enriching the data with human-understandable semantics. A dual-level contrastive learning strategy aligns raw and textual features both within and across modalities, mitigating semantic gaps and enhancing multimodal consistency. Spatial dependencies are modeled through a graph attention network, and temporal dynamics are captured via a transformer encoder to produce 24-hour mobility sequences. Results from Shenzhen demonstrate that LMEMR outperforms the baseline CLIP model, achieving an $R^{2}$ of 0.856 and an 18.07% reduction in MAE. Ablation experiments confirm the effectiveness of semantic enhancement, spatial graph reasoning, and cross-modal fusion. Overall, this research reveals the potential of static multimodal data for dynamic mobility inference, offering a scalable, interpretable, and privacy-friendly solution for smart city planning and management.

title: Dense-Seg: A Ground Segmentation Method for Dense Point Clouds Based on Triangular Node Representation
authors: Eksan Firkat, Tayir Mijit, Pakzada Jilil, Bin Zhu, Enyong Xu, Jihong Zhu, Askar Hamdulla
abstract: In autonomous driving technology, accurate ground segmentation of LiDAR data is critical for effective path planning and decision-making. While existing state-of-the-art algorithms have demonstrated compatibility with high-resolution LiDAR systems, comprehensive evaluation and optimal processing of dense 128-channel point clouds across diverse, complex terrains remain an open research challenge. These methods often face trade-offs between computational efficiency and precise boundary retention in non-planar environments. To address this pressing issue, this paper presents Dense-Seg, an innovative general-purpose ground segmentation method tailored for high-resolution LiDAR, with exceptional robustness in complex and unstructured off-road environments. The proposed methodology consists of four synergistic stages. First, a Triangular Node Representation (TNR) encodes the 3-D scene into a regular triangular mesh, reducing the search space and enabling real-time processing. Second, Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-based initial ground segmentation is applied within each node to obtain coarse ground and non-ground points via plane fitting. Third, elevation value-based ground optimization utilizes the Elevation Features of Point Clouds within Nodes (EFPN)—height difference and variance—to correct slope-induced misclassifications. Finally, the Geometric Features of Adjacent Nodes (GFAN) are leveraged through conditional filtering, propagating labels to the most linear neighbor to refine boundaries at plane intersections. This integrated approach significantly improves the precision and reliability of ground segmentation, delivering 83.2 % F1-score and 80.1 % mIoU on the 128-channel GOOSE dataset while maintaining 22 ms per-frame runtime on a single Central Processing Unit (CPU)—outperforming existing classical methods and enabling robust perception for high-resolution autonomous driving systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/Eksanf/DenseSeg

title: Reaction-Aware Planning With Preference Cost Learning for Human-Like Autonomous Driving in Unsignalized Intersections
authors: Heng Deng, Nuoyan Chen, Jingyuan Zhan, Liguo Zhang
abstract: Planning tasks for unsignalized intersection scenarios present significant challenges due to the frequent interactions required with surrounding vehicles. Most autonomous driving systems often treat prediction and planning as two sequential and independent tasks, which fails to predict other participants’ reactions to the ego-vehicle’s actions. For such a purpose, this paper proposes a reaction-aware planning framework using Transformer to model the interactions between traffic participants and the ego-vehicle, and employs preference cost learning in the decision-making stage to learn the latent pReferences of human drivers for trajectory decisions from samples. Our method is validated through closed-loop simulations utilizing the nuplan dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves improved performance in unsignalized intersection scenarios compared to other methods, and exhibits driving behaviors that more closely align with those of human drivers.

title: An End-to-End GPS-Based Traffic Speed Prediction Framework Without Explicit Map-Matching
authors: Beiyu Song, Yu Yang, Tingting Fan, Hongbo Ye, Edward Chung, Jiannong Cao
abstract: Traffic speed prediction is crucial in traffic management and vehicle routing by forecasting future speeds on urban roads using historical and real-time traffic data. Vehicle trajectories provide valuable spatial-temporal insights into city-wide traffic patterns, and thus are important in modeling speed dynamics. However, existing trajectory-based traffic prediction methods rely heavily on map-matching, which requires extensive GPS data preprocessing and introduces potential errors and uncertainties, particularly in dense road networks with long gaps between recorded locations. In this study, we propose GT-Net, an end-to-end GPS-based traffic prediction network that eliminates the need for map-matching. GT-Net initially reorganizes traffic speed data at the segment level to capture spatial-temporal intercorrelations. It then employs a GPS-to-Road attention network to estimate the likelihood of road matches while preserving the sequential orders of trajectory points. Additionally, a time-aware attention-based trajectory network is designed to approximate the driver’s likely path, effectively modeling the impact of varying driving patterns on traffic speed dynamics. GT-Net outperforms state-of-the-art approaches and also demonstrates strong robustness based on extensive experiments conducted on a large city-scale real-world dataset with significant GPS drift.

title: Research on the Multi-Target Perception Capability of mmWave Radar in Complex Traffic Environments
authors: Bin Li, Tao Li, Yi Yang, Shuang Zhang, Jiashuai Chen, Xiaolei Dong, Geng Luo
abstract: This paper addresses the need for multi-target detection using vehicle-mounted millimeter-wave radar in complex traffic scenarios such as dense traffic flow, multipath effects, and mutual interference. It constructs an edge-side real-time perception system based on AWR2944 and proposes an AE-CFAR detection framework. The system employs a $3\mathrm {Tx}\times 4\mathrm {Rx}$ array to form 12 virtual channels, generating 120 electronic beams within a ±30° field of view to construct a range–Doppler–angle three-dimensional data cube. A lightweight autoencoder is used to learn background reconstructable patterns, and CFAR threshold judgment is performed in the residual energy domain to improve detection stability under conditions of non-uniform clutter and dense targets. Verification through four types of experiments—anechoic chamber, urban vehicle-mounted, artificial smoke, and high-speed gantry—shows that: the detection rate remains above 92% under dense working conditions (number of targets > 40); the pedestrian detection rate is approximately 87% when visibility is 5 m (while cameras are below 40%); the detection rate for gantries at 0–200 m is above 93%, and remains above 90% beyond 200 m; the end-to-end latency P95 is approximately 68 ms, beamforming takes about 0.8 ms per frame, and AE inference time after INT8 quantization is less than 5 ms per frame, meeting the real-time budget for on-vehicle online deployment.

title: A Survey on End-to-End Autonomous Driving Training From the Perspectives of Data, Strategy, and Platform

title: CD-SAC: Constant Distance With Speed Adjustment in Curves for Non-Column Vehicle Platoon Control
authors: Constance Hendrix, Gedare Bloom
abstract: Unmanned ground vehicle platoons are not constrained to travel in columns on well-marked roads. Allowing lateral inter-vehicle spacing creates unique challenges compared with highway driving in restricted column formations. These challenges include the absence of road markings and planned trajectories along with differences in velocity and position keeping while turning. In this paper, we introduce a real-time velocity adjustment based on turning radius for non-column formations that addresses the discrepancy in matching velocities in a turn. Two non-column formations are evaluated over two network topologies with varying connectivity using a two-dimensional scenario which simultaneously invokes an acceleration and a heading change using a dynamic three-degree-of-freedom vehicle model. A velocity adjustment is made in curves where predecessors are laterally offset with the ego vehicle. If the predecessor’s turning radius is smaller (larger), the ego vehicle’s velocity increases (decreases). This novel adjustment is a deviation from the status quo where competing control actions exist between maintaining a constant inter-vehicle spacing and matching velocities in curves. Experimental results using this novel velocity adjustment show a maximum 74% decrease in longitudinal distance error, a maximum 94% decrease in lateral distance error across platoon followers and a significant reduction in standard deviation across platoon members along experimental path trajectories.

title: RT-RIDMOS: Real-Time Railway Intrusion Detection Method Based on Moving Object Segmentation
authors: Yongbo Wu, Ziyang Feng, Xinyu Zhu, Ping Tan, Huoping Yi, Jin Ding, Zhen Li, Jien Ma
abstract: Railway intrusions, characterized by their unpredictable and sudden nature, pose a significant threat to operational safety in railway transportation. While recent breakthroughs in computer vision have substantially advanced intrusion detection algorithms, two fundamental challenges persist: the paucity of labeled intrusion samples, which severely constrains the performance and generalization of supervised models, and the limitation of existing methods to predefined object categories, rendering them ineffective against unknown threats. Therefore, this paper introduces RT-RIDMOS, an innovative real-time moving object segmentation method tailored for railway intrusion detection. At the input stage, the Spatio-Temporal Contextual Fusion (STCF) module equips the model with rich, multi-scale spatiotemporal information. This enables the network to segment intruding objects based on their motion discrepancy against the static background, rather than relying on appearance features. Consequently, our approach fundamentally circumvents the dependency on large-scale, category-annotated datasets, achieving robust, category-agnostic detection of arbitrary intruding objects. Furthermore, to satisfy the stringent real-time requirements for edge deployment while maintaining high performance, we have meticulously designed a lightweight backbone with a large receptive field. Extensive experiments on our custom-built, real-world railway intrusion dataset demonstrate the superiority of our method. With a remarkably low parameter count of only 1.12M, RT-RIDMOS achieves a state-of-the-art (SOTA) F-measure of 0.826. It significantly outperforms existing methods in model size, memory footprint, and inference speed, highlighting its considerable potential for continuous and efficient deployment on railway edge AI devices.

title: Decentralized Learning for Multi-UAV Rail-Line Inspection With Imperfect Information: A Fictitious Self-Play Approach
authors: Yin Jia, Li Zhu, F. Richard Yu, Bo Ai, Tao Tang
abstract: Rail-line inspection is essential for the stable operation of rail transit systems. Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV) swarms are increasingly deployed for large-scale rail-line inspection, where efficient coordination and intelligent resource management are critical. However, most existing methods unrealistically assume complete global information and centralized control, which fails to hold in practical rail transit inspection scenarios where imperfect information arises from limited communication bandwidth and private UAV states. To address this challenge, we model the cooperative rail-line inspection problem as a stochastic game with imperfect information and propose a decentralized learning framework, termed Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle Fictitious Self-Play (U-FSP). Each UAV models its decision process as a belief-augmented Markov Decision Process (MDP) and iteratively learns equilibrium strategies through alternating best-response learning and policy averaging. We theoretically prove that the formulated rail-line inspection game constitutes an exact potential game, guaranteeing convergence of U-FSP to the Nash equilibrium. Simulation results in rail-line inspection environments demonstrate that U-FSP significantly reduces UAV energy consumption and task completion delay, mitigates resource congestion while maximizing overall rewards under imperfect information. Furthermore, analytical experiments show that U-FSP drives the rail-line inspection system toward a Nash equilibrium.

title: Dwelling and Speed Advisory Enhanced Max-Pressure Control With Transit Signal Priority
authors: Chaopeng Tan, Georgios Laskaris, Dingshan Sun, Robin Abohariri, Marco Rinaldi, Hans van Lint
abstract: Max-Pressure (MP) control is a decentralized real-time traffic signal control method that is popular for its simplicity and theoretical stability. However, most existing MP controllers prioritize throughput for private vehicles without accounting for the specific needs of transit services that are essential for sustainable urban mobility. This oversight can exacerbate transit delays and undermine the effectiveness of public transportation systems. To address these challenges, this study introduces a Priority-MP framework that integrates transit signal priority and driver advisory systems into MP control for multi-modal traffic networks. By weighting pressures based on real-time vehicle occupancy and considering more realistic scenarios that account for the presence of transit stations, Priority-MP prioritizes high-occupancy transit vehicles while ensuring network queue stability. In addition, the framework integrates driver advisory systems to provide speed and dwell time recommendations for transit vehicles. Experiments on a real-world multi-modal traffic corridor in Amsterdam show that compared to existing MP control methods: 1) Priority-MP highlights an important trade-off: it significantly reduces average passenger delay by prioritizing high-occupancy transit vehicles, even though this may lead to increased average vehicle delay when the impact of transit stations are ignored; 2) Priority-MP considering transit stations reduces both vehicle delay and passenger delay while maintaining the network stability; and 3) Priority-MP integrating driver advisory systems further improves the travel smoothness of transit vehicles by reducing transit queuing counts.

title: Bi-Level Auction-Based Platoon Control for Signal-Free Intersections
authors: Christina Iliopoulou, Emmanouil Kampitakis, Eleni I. Vlahogianni
abstract: This study presents a bi-level auction-based framework for coordinated platoon control at signal-free intersections, leveraging the capabilities of Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) and vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication. Unlike traditional road pricing mechanisms, which lack individual differentiation and responsiveness to local congestion, the proposed framework enables dynamic and equitable traffic management by incorporating vehicle-level valuations of travel time. At the upper level, vehicle requests are grouped in non-conflicting movements, and a Sponsored Search Auction (SSA) determines the priority sequence based on individual bids and proximity to the intersection. At the lower level, an optimization model jointly determines the optimal platoon speeds and lengths, allowing for platoon splitting when necessary. A mixed-integer nonlinear formulation is developed and relaxed for efficient solution. The proposed mechanism ensures efficiency and fairness, addressing the coordination challenges arising from heterogeneous platoon preferences. Integrated into the SUMO microscopic simulation platform, the framework demonstrates significant improvements in intersection efficiency and equity compared to conventional methods, offering a scalable and adaptive approach to traffic coordination in CAV-only environments.

title: A Review of Vision-Based Vehicle Detection for UAV-Based Traffic Monitoring: Experimental Insights and Future Directions
authors: Jianlin Ye, Christos Kyrkou
abstract: In Intelligent Transportation System (ITS), uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-based surveillance offers an innovative solution to traffic surveillance with wide coverage and real-time data collection capabilities. In comparison to fixed ground-based infrastructure, UAVs are able to respond to dynamic traffic but present challenges such as vehicle detection at varying altitudes, compensation for motion-induced image variations and efficient processing of high-resolution images. Deep learning has been largely beneficial on improving the detection accuracy; however, for practical deployment, a critical assessment of the accuracy, latency, and harmonization with current transportation systems needs to be carefully considered. This survey reviews recent advancements in the UAV-based traffic monitoring, with a primary focus being deep neural network models for traffic analytics in various urban settings. Three main challenges identified in the literature are ensuring compatibility with traffic control systems, achieving real-time processing to optimize traffic flow, and maintaining robust detection in different environmental conditions. Existing solutions often lack comprehensive frameworks for utilizing UAV captured data to respond to incidents and manage traffic effectively. Future research should focus on optimal detection models, edge processing, and adaptive control integration to improve the responsiveness of urban traffic management.

title: Low-Latency Object Detection in Driving Scenes: A Hybrid Spiking Neural Network for Motion-Compensated Fusion
authors: Zhonghui Han, Xinhao Luo, Jianwu Fang, Yuning Wang, Guoqi Li, Jianru Xue
abstract: Event camera recently is treated as a promising complementary visual sensor to overcome the perception challenges posed by complex lighting and high-speed traffic scenarios besetting the RGB cameras, and derives many event-RGB modality fusion approaches. However, the temporal synchronization between event streams and RGB frames is still a pending problem influencing on the high-performance and low-latency scene perception. In this work, we propose LOD-Drive, a hybrid spiking neural network for low-latency asynchronous object detection in driving scenes, which leverages the energy-efficient encoding capability of spiking neural networks (SNNs) to extract and maintain the high-frequency motion information from event streams. The spike-propagated motion features are asynchronously aligned with RGB motion flow for compensating the motion discrepancies within two modalities. Specifically, we propose a hybrid motion-guided temporal alignment module that encodes motion cues from event data to adaptively calibrate RGB features at the current timestamp, and the temporally aligned RGB features and event features are fused via a spatio-temporal cross-modal attention module with a decoder to output the final detections. Extensive experiment evaluations demonstrate that LOD-Drive significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on DSEC-Detection and PKU-DAVIS-SOD datasets.

title: DINO-CoDT: Multi-Class Collaborative Detection and VFM-Guided Tracking

title: Occlusion Handling for Intelligent Vehicles Using Audio-Visual Multi-Object Tracking
authors: Thushara R. Bandara, Amirali K. Gostar, Prarthana Abeysinghe, Ehsan Asadi, Reza Hoseinnezhad
abstract: This paper proposes a novel multi-object tracking framework for intelligent vehicles, addressing the challenge of maintaining situational awareness during visual occlusions, where objects may be fully or partially blocked by other vehicles, infrastructure, or environmental elements. We first evaluate a visual-only tracking pipeline using static birth modeling and extend it with adaptive birth to compensate for missed detections; however, both approaches struggle to maintain tracks through occlusion events. Extending our previous work on audio–visual fusion, this study introduces a non-traditional, data-driven audio likelihood function that operates directly on raw microphone array signals in a track-before-detect (TBD) manner. Unlike conventional approaches relying on preprocessed direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimates, the proposed likelihood is computed using the Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC)-based spatial spectrum analysis and formulated as a Gaussian mixture. Audio measurements are incorporated into a Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) implementation of the Labeled Multi-Bernoulli (LMB) filter, and the resulting visual and audio posteriors, obtained after independent LMB updates, are fused using Generalized Covariance Intersection (GCI). A physics-based simulation framework is developed to generate realistic vehicle acoustic signals and evaluate performance under two urban traffic scenarios with varying interaction density (moderate and dense). Monte Carlo experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently improves tracking accuracy, cardinality estimation, and robustness compared to visual-only baselines. The results highlight the effectiveness of signal-level audio–visual fusion in maintaining track continuity under prolonged occlusions and increased scene complexity.

title: PanSR: An Object-Centric Mask Transformer for Maritime Panoptic Segmentation
authors: Lojze Zust, Matej Kristan
abstract: Environmental panoptic perception and obstacle detection are key components in enabling autonomy for autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs). Recent studies have demonstrated that general panoptic methods, currently dominated by mask transformer approaches, are unsuitable for maritime environments, as they perform poorly in crowded scenes and in scenes with a wide range of object scales, highlighting the need for domain-specific panoptic methods. In this work, we identify several fundamental shortcomings of these recent methods and rethink architecture design choices from the perspective of perception for autonomous navigation. We introduce PanSR, a new panoptic segmentation method with the following main contributions: 1) an object-centric proposal extraction module for better handling of object size variety, 2) an improved ground-truth matching scheme consistent with proposal extraction, and 3) object-centric mask prediction for better instance separation of similar objects. With these enhancements, PanSR effectively mitigates instance merging, enhances small-object detection and increases performance in crowded scenes, delivering a notable +3.4% PQ improvement over state-of-the-art on the challenging LaRS benchmark and +8.4% PQ on WaterScenes, while retaining competitive performance on the autonomous driving perception benchmark Cityscapes. The code and models are publicly available on GitHub.

title: Adap-STWT: Real-Time Traffic Flow Prediction Based on Multi-Scale Graph Adaptive Fusion and Spatio-Temporal Wavelet Transformer
authors: Shijie Cai, Jie Hu, Jia Chen, Wencai Xu
abstract: Accurate traffic prediction is crucial for managing and making decisions in urban traffic systems. Recent studies have shown outstanding performance in traffic prediction by using methods that employ graph adjacency matrices predefined by heuristic rules or learn graph structures through trainable parameters. These studies tend to focus on interactions between nodes based on macroscopic traffic node attributes, overlooking the profound impact of individual behaviors and decisions of microscopic traffic participants on the transportation system. This valuable microscopic information has not been utilized to guide graph structure learning. In this paper, we proposed a spatio-temporal model with the capability of multi-scale adaptive graph structure learning, named Adap-STWT. Initially, an optimal graph structure learning module is constructed for dynamic traffic systems, encompassing multiple scales from microscopic traffic participants to macroscopic node attributes. Subsequently, in conjunction with this optimal graph structure, an optimized spatio-temporal prediction module is designed to facilitate multi-step traffic flow prediction. Ultimately, iterative optimization of the two modules is achieved through an alternating training approach. Notably, owing to the limited availability of large-scale public traffic datasets containing trajectory information, evaluations are conducted on two relatively small public datasets. The results underscore the potential of graph structure learning based on microscopic trajectories for traffic flow prediction. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/caisj11/Adap-STWT.git

title: Integrated Planning of Virtual Coupling Train Convoy Formation Schemes and Timetables With Dynamic Coupling–Decoupling

title: Analyzing the Impact of Service Stages on Demand and Modal Shift for Urban Air Mobility: A Case Study of Seoul Metropolitan Area
authors: Hyunsoo Kim, Kwanjung Yee
abstract: Upon the introduction of urban air mobility (UAM) services as a new transportation mode, a substantial portion of demand is expected to be generated by passengers shifting from conventional transportation modes. However, previous studies have focused on the primary mode of transportation that shifts to UAM in specific service stages, overlooking how modal shift patterns evolve as the service matures. Additionally, most prior studies have reported only total demand values, without distinguishing between different types of routes such as airport shuttles and local intra-city trips, which obscures route-specific demand characteristics. This study aims to bridge this gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of mode choice patterns and route characteristics for UAM services throughout the entire service stages. A utility-based mode choice model is applied, and a case study of the Seoul metropolitan area is conducted using empirical travel data. The results indicate that as UAM services mature, targeting the demand shift from private vehicle users has more potential to generate high demand than targeting public transport or taxi users. Furthermore, the findings indicate that routes with high demand during a specific service stage do not consistently follow high demand throughout the entire service stage. In particular, airport routes initially show higher modal shift rates due to greater time savings, their influence on overall UAM demand diminishes over time because of their inherently low traffic volume. These findings offer practical insights for policy-makers and planners, particularly in cities with mobility patterns similar to Seoul, by supporting strategic decisions on service planning and infrastructure development.

title: S2R: From Screening to Recognition, Event-Driven Perception of Railway Defects in Low-Power Systems
authors: Mingxu Li, Donghai Zhai, Shichun Wang
abstract: Automated, real-time inspection of railway infrastructure is critical for ensuring the safety of modern transportation systems. Deploying such perception systems on edge devices, however, is constrained by stringent power limitations. While Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are well-suited for low-power sensing, their non-differentiable spiking dynamics complicate direct training. In contrast, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) achieve easier optimization convergence but incur sustained high-power computational requirements, making them ill-suited for continuous and off-grid monitoring. Thus, integrating a shallow SNN for simple yet high-frequency tasks with a deep ANN for more complex tasks emerges as a promising solution. In this work, we propose an event-driven perception framework for railway surface defect segmentation to enable real-time railway defect inspection in edge deployments. The SNN serves as a region proposal module to detect potential defects, and only the defective segments are forwarded to the ANN for finer segmentation. This design enables our model to achieve high performance on sparse target inspection tasks with minimal energy consumption. We also collected and annotated a dataset named DeTian Railway Surface Defect (DTRSD), comprising 1,126 real-world railway defect images captured under diverse natural lighting conditions. These images capture anomalies, such as dust deposits and rust stains, offering a realistic environment for evaluating segmentation methods. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves competitive accuracy while reducing energy consumption relative to existing approaches. The code and dataset will be publicly available at https://github.com/lidadadaxu/HybridRSD

title: W-Diffusion: A Probabilistic Generative Framework for Traffic Forecasting via Shallow Diffusion Mechanism
authors: Zhepu Yang, Shuangxun Ma, Tao Dai, Peixin Chen, Ruixuan Zhang, Daniel Jian Sun, Xiangmo Zhao, Shirui Pan
abstract: Timely-accurate traffic forecasting is crucial for urban traffic guidance and control. Accurate forecasting of traffic flow and speed are essential for analyzing road usage, alleviating congestion, and enabling real-time monitoring and dynamic navigation. These capabilities contribute to enhanced road safety and more efficient infrastructure operation. Most existing methods neglect the inherent uncertainties within the traffic scenario, which reduces their practicality for real-world traffic control. The newly emerged denoising diffusion probabilistic models bring new inspiration to address this issue. However, these models only involve a single generation process, which is not appropriate for traffic forecasting task. Furthermore, the impact of Gaussian noise in generative process brings more challenges for modeling signal correlations. To overcome these limitations, we present the first attempt to introduce the shallow diffusion mechanism into traffic forecasting task, leading to a novel framework called W-Diffusion. The proposed model consists of separated shallow and deep diffusion stages, in order to better capture the signal correlations during the generative process. We also devise a new denoising network AST-Unet, to combine the spatiotemporal learning capabilities of spatiotemporal graph neural networks with the uncertainty measurements of diffusion models. Comprehensive experimental evaluations are conducted on the Caltrans Performance Measurement System (PeMS) benchmarks to validate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

title: U3A: Uncertainty-Aware Accident Anticipation for Reliable Autonomous Driving
authors: Xingcheng Liu, Bin Rao, Yanchen Guan, Wanping Liu, Chengyue Wang, Xuesong Wang, Dengbo He, Yang Liu, Zhenning Li, Keqiang Li, Chengzhong Xu

title: DSTIGFN: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Interactive Graph Fusion Network for Traffic Flow Prediction
authors: Shiqi Zhang, Zhen Liu, Yuzhuang Pian, Jialong Qian, Yonghong Liu, H. Oliver Gao
abstract: Accurate traffic flow prediction is crucial for the efficient management of urban transportation systems. However, existing models generally focus on modeling continuous traffic sequences, ignoring the multilevel correlation characteristics of spatio-temporal heterogeneity in traffic networks at different time scales. Moreover, the spatial dependencies among road nodes are usually modeled by static graphs, making it difficult to capture their dynamic evolution over time. To address the above challenges, this paper proposes a Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Interactive Graph Fusion Network. First, the model periodically encodes the original traffic flow sequence to extract the periodic patterns and global temporal structures embedded in it. Building on this foundation, a trend-preserving parity decomposition is applied to divide the time series into odd and even subsequences, preserving temporal trends while introducing diverse temporal perspectives to support multi-scale temporal modeling. For each subsequence, adaptive and supra-Laplacian graph structures are constructed to capture evolving spatial dependencies and deep temporal correlations. Graph convolution and a subgraph interaction fusion strategy are then employed to integrate complementary information across subsequences. Finally, by restoring the odd and even subsequence features to their original temporal order, the model effectively integrates global and local spatio-temporal dependencies, thereby enhancing its ability to predict complex traffic patterns. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zachary-Qi/DSTIGFN-master

title: Safety-Critical Space-and-Time-Synchronized Cooperative Formation: Virtual-Structure-Based Framework
authors: Peng Wang, Weilin Cheng, Xiuhui Peng, Haibin Wang, Weidong Zhang
abstract: This paper proposes a three-dimensional (3D) safety-critical cooperative guidance and control strategy for a group of vehicles aiming at simultaneous formation around a target. First, a reference relative trajectory is constructed using piecewise B $\acute {e}$ zier curves to define a time-independent spatial path, along which a space-and-time synchronization strategy is employed to ensure that all vehicles reach their designated relative positions simultaneously. Next, the dimensionless residual path and velocity in reference relative motion are taken as coordination variables in the space-and-time-synchronized cooperative guidance, and a distributed coordination strategy with upper and lower bound constraints on path velocity is designed. Finally, fixed-time controllers with integrated extended state observers (ESOs) are designed for kinematic and kinetic systems to track the reference trajectory under control saturation, while safety constraints are enforced via control barrier function (CBF)-based compensation. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed cooperative guidance law.

title: Improved Soft Actor-Critic for Unmanned Underwater Vehicle Obstacle Avoidance
authors: Bo Zhong, Hongjian Wang, Zhenwei Lu, Yutong Huang, Jingfei Ren
abstract: Traditional collision avoidance methods for unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) are highly dependent on the measurement accuracy of sensors and environmental maps and perform poorly in unknown dynamic environments. To improve the generalization ability of the UUV collision avoidance method when there is no prior knowledge of the underwater environment and sonar observation is uncertain, an improved soft actor-critic (SAC) method is proposed in this work. The improved SAC network architecture includes an encoder layer, a dynamic feature layer, and a merge layer. The long short-term memory (LSTM) network is integrated into the dynamic feature layer to capture historical state spaces and action spaces, and improve the collision policy’s memory capability. In this method, the state space is composed of forward-looking sonar perception, UUV motion state, and relative target position. In addition, to enhance the training efficiency and stability of the improved SAC, we design the continuous state space, the action space, and a composite reward function. We built a simulation platform and demonstrated that the improved SAC could effectively complete autonomous collision avoidance in environments with static and dynamic obstacles under external disturbances. The improved method enables the UUV to reach the target faster and reduces the path length and decision-making time of collision avoidance.

title: Interpretable Symbolic Regression for Spatio-Temporal Traffic Prediction
authors: Mingxi Li, Zhengmin Shi, Guoyang Qin, Wei Ma
abstract: Interpretable traffic prediction uncovers the dynamics of traffic variations in transportation networks, making it essential for accurate decision-making in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). However, widely-used methods, particularly those based on deep learning, often function as black-box models, limiting their interpretability and efficiency. To address this limitation, we propose an interpretable symbolic regression model for traffic prediction, StSr, achieving state-of-the-art performance while maintaining interpretability. Symbolic regression derives interpretable mathematical expressions directly from data, eliminating the need for predefined functional forms while employing gradient-free optimization to capture nonlinear relationships and perform feature selection, and fine-tune the free coefficients. Despite its generalizability, symbolic regression avoids abundant model structures, input, and reduces the computation complexity while maintaining excellent prediction performance. Notably, StSr leverages parallelism on CPUs to enhance computational efficiency and scalability, reducing reliance on GPU resources and making the model particularly effective for complex prediction tasks. The model’s novel end-to-end architecture comprises two key stages: the initial stage searches for the structure of prediction functions, and the subsequent stage optimizes the free coefficients within these structures. Discrete optimization is used for structure seeking, followed by continuous optimization for coefficient optimization. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through extensive experiments on various real-world traffic speed and flow datasets, demonstrating its ability to enhance performance and computational efficiency.

title: Multi-Tier Autonomous Ride Services: A Systematic Analysis of Fleet Providers' Pricing Strategies
authors: Daniel Mawunyo Doe, Xiangfang Li, Yuqing Hu, Zhu Han, Lijun Qian
abstract: This paper presents an analytical framework for optimal pricing and service design in multi-tier autonomous ride services, with premium and standard tiers, under monopoly and duopoly market structures. Users choose among tiers by jointly considering fares, expected wait times, and service quality, which leads to closed-form thresholds for premium–standard indifference, ride feasibility, and a critical impatience level that determines tier viability. The monopoly case is modeled as a three-stage Stackelberg game, which yields midpoint pricing rules and a condition under which a standard-only configuration maximizes profit when the premium cost markup is high. We analyze the duopoly case using the two-stage Bertrand (price competition) and Cournot (capacity competition) games, with unique equilibria characterized and comparative statics provided over trip distance, operating cost, cost ratio, and rider valuation. Results show that price competition increases user payoff, participation, and social welfare relative to Cournot and monopoly, while provider profit follows the opposite ordering (monopoly greater than Cournot greater than Bertrand). Multi-tier offerings can outperform single-tier strategies by endogenously segmenting riders when the gain from premium segmentation exceeds the associated cannibalization loss. A publicly observable Tesla–Waymo price snapshot is used as a real-world market illustration that provides preliminary empirical grounding for the model’s pricing insights, highlighting price-driven inclusion versus capacity- and cost-driven pricing. The framework yields threshold-based decision rules for when premium service is viable, when standard-only provision dominates, and how pricing responds to trip length, delay sensitivity, and operating cost.

title: Impacts of Heterogeneous Traffic Environments on Vehicle-Infrastructure Collaborative Computing Latency: A Multi-Layer Agent-Based Simulation Approach
authors: Xinyun Lao, Yu Shen, Difei Wu, Gang Liu, Yuchuan Du
abstract: Achieving efficient task offloading with low latency in cooperative vehicle-infrastructure systems represents a critical challenge influenced by three key factors: heterogeneous vehicle computational capabilities, dynamic traffic conditions, and variable communication reliability. To address the fundamental trade-off between real-time processing performance and cost-effective infrastructure investment, this study develops a multi-layer agent-based modeling (ABM) framework that systematically evaluates how roadside unit (RSU) computation capacity, traffic volume, and vehicular computation capability (VCC) heterogeneity collectively impact collaborative computing latency. The ABM framework comprises three interconnected layers: an infrastructure layer that models RSUs with sensing, communication, and computing functions; a traffic layer that simulates diverse traffic environments; and a collaborative computing layer that manages decentralized task generation and offloading. A modified water-filling algorithm is integrated to dynamically allocate computational tasks based on available resources and latency constraints. Simulation results under signalized intersection scenarios reveal nonlinear latency growth with increasing traffic volume due to queuing effects. When the RSU computing capacity is insufficient, most tasks are offloaded to nearby vehicles. Our results show that when the RSU computational capacity is comparable to the total VCC of all vehicles, the RSU processes approximately 40% of the tasks, primarily due to vehicle–RSU mobility effects and stochastic wireless transmission failures. Furthermore, increasing VCC heterogeneity—while keeping the average constant—leads to both higher average latency and greater variability. These findings provide quantitative insights for optimizing computing resource deployment in real-world cooperative systems.

title: CmIVTP: Cross-Modal Interaction-Based Vessel Trajectory Prediction for Maritime Intelligence
authors: Yuxu Lu, Dong Yang, Xiaoyu Li, Mengwei Bao, Congcong Zhao
abstract: Maritime intelligent transportation systems (MITS) are essential for ensuring navigation safety and efficiency in busy waterways. However, accurate vessel trajectory prediction remains challenging due to the limitations of single-source data. Automatic identification system (AIS) data is often sparse or unavailable for small vessels, while closed-circuit television (CCTV) data alone cannot fully capture dynamic vessel behavior. To mitigate these challenges, we propose a cross-modal interaction-based vessel trajectory prediction (named CmIVTP) framework to model the intricate interactions between vessel dynamics and environmental constraints. Specifically, we introduce a target-aware scene encoder to extract scene semantic features, effectively capturing vessel-environment interactions and enhancing trajectory prediction accuracy. In addition, we propose a cross-modal interaction transformer, which integrates AIS-derived motion features, CCTV-based environmental features, and scene representations. It leverages cross-modal attention mechanisms to simultaneously capture intra-modal semantics and inter-modal interactions, ensuring dynamically consistent and environmentally feasible predictions. Furthermore, we construct a vessel group trajectory bank by clustering historical AIS trajectories into representative motion patterns, providing an efficient and scalable approach for candidate trajectory generation. Additionally, we introduce the maritime multimodal dataset plus (named Maritime-MmD$^+$), a large-scale dataset that synchronizes AIS data and CCTV video data, providing robust support for multimodal trajectory prediction research. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CmIVTP achieves better performance on multimodal-driven vessel trajectory prediction benchmarks. The code resources for this work can be available at https://github.com/LouisYxLu/CmIVTP.

title: Pride and Prejudice: Toward an Information-Theoretic Framework for Mutually Communicative Driver Behavior Modeling
authors: Tingjun Li, Nan Xu, Shuo Feng, Hassan Askari, Bruno Henrique Groenner Barbosa, Konghui Guo
abstract: Mixed autonomy driving becomes unsafe and inefficient when autonomous vehicles (AVs) and human-driven vehicles (HVs) misread each other's intentions. We study this problem as implicit mutual communication in lane changes. The proposed framework models how the ego vehicle both expresses its intent and probes the other driver's preference under epistemic uncertainty. It combines a level-k Bayesian persuasion game with virtual features for proactive signaling, information-theoretic rewards for mutual communication, and adaptive weights of communication affordances. We further introduce the Pride-Inquiry (P-I) and Pride-Prejudice (P-P) planes to analyze communication intensity and tendency. The model is calibrated with a Communication-Based Multi-Agent Inverse Reinforcement Learning algorithm (C-MIRL) on the naturalistic NGSIM dataset. Compared with the non-communicative baseline, the proposed model reduces the prediction error of mandatory lane changes by up to 20% while maintaining strong generalization. Driver-In-the-Loop questionnaire scores are positively correlated with the calibrated communication variables, supporting the subjective validity of the model. The learned rewards further show that inquiry and listening affordances contribute more than pride and expression alone, and that inquiry preference varies more strongly across drivers. These results support explicit modeling of mutual communication and epistemic uncertainty in interactive driving.

title: An Optimized Collaborative Routing Model for Trucks and Heterogeneous Drones in Delivery and Pickup Services
authors: Biao Xu, Qiwen Lu, Xiaozhi Gao, Bing Li, Wenji Li, Jie He, Dunwei Gong, Zhun Fan
abstract: Addressing the “last mile” logistics challenge, this paper proposes a truck and heterogeneous drones collaborative routing problem (HCRP-DP) to efficiently meet the growing customer demands for delivery and pickup services at the lowest cost. An adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm based on the simulated annealing framework (ALNS-SA), is designed to solve HCRP-DP. It incorporates asynchronous drone operations and heterogeneous drone characteristics, with seven destructive operators and a heuristic repair operator to explore the solution space and speed up local search convergence. Comparatively, ALNS-SA significantly outperforms a state-of-the-art algorithm in convergence. The HCRP-DP model not only reduces service costs but also offers insights into how varying customer proportions affect model performance, providing valuable practical application guidance.

title: Evaluating Multi-Modal UAM Impacts at Metro Region Scale: A San Francisco Bay Area Study
authors: Xin Peng, Xuan Jiang, Vishwanath Bulusu, Emin Burak Onat, Raja Sengupta
abstract: This paper presents a method for evaluating and analyzing the effect of multi-modal Urban Air Mobility (UAM) operations on passenger travel time and the ground transportation system in a metropolitan region. The proposed method comprises a vertiport network design module, a graphical-processing-unit-based (GPU-based) micro-simulator for modeling vehicle movements, and a UAM allocator. We perform a hierarchical vertiport network design to determine vertiport placement and passenger assignment. With an ultra-fast parallelized micro-simulator, we simulate passenger movement and measure changes in traffic network congestion in the presence of UAM operations. We apply the proposed method to 9 million driving trips, representing roughly half-day demand in the San Francisco Bay Area, and estimate UAM and non-UAM passenger travel time changes by providing UAM service. Assuming that passengers use UAM if there is a travel time saving, the results showed a reduction of up to 37.07% of total Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT). The changes in the average travel speed of the road network and the travel time of non-UAM passengers also showed a reduction in ground congestion, although with a significant number of vertiports. An infrastructure analysis to better understand the comparative value of the land showed that UAM, as part of a multimodal system, could move more people per unit of land area compared to existing urban land-based transit options in the study region.

title: MSFormer: Multi-Scale Transformer With Hierarchical and Local Awareness for Traffic Flow Prediction
authors: Shilong Dong, Shengjie Zhao, Jiafeng Huang, Kenan Ye, Wenzhen Jia
abstract: Traffic flow prediction, a key technology in intelligent transportation systems, has seen rapid advancements over the past few decades. Recent studies have widely applied Transformers in this field, owing to their effectiveness in modeling complex spatial and temporal dependencies in traffic data. However, existing methods still fall short in capturing the intrinsic characteristics of traffic systems, mainly due to two limitations: 1) limited capability to capture the hierarchy of spatial information from multiple scales, including semantic and geographic aspects; and 2) an excessive focus on global information while neglecting dynamic local relations between nodes. To address these issues, we propose a Multi-Scale transFormer (MSFormer) that extracts the semantic and geographic hierarchy of road networks while fully capturing dynamic local relations between sensors. Specifically, MSFormer consists of two key components: 1) a clustering-based spatial hierarchical segmentation module that captures semantic and geographical hierarchies by jointly leveraging traffic patterns and network topology; and 2) a multi-scale spatial encoder containing a dynamic local awareness module. The multi-scale spatial encoder integrates information across different levels to enhance intra-region coherence and capture inter-region dependencies, while the dynamic local awareness mechanism models the evolution of local relations via short-term traffic pattern similarity. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that MSFormer outperforms competitive baselines, confirming its effectiveness in capturing hierarchical structures and dynamic local relations for improved traffic flow prediction. The source code is available at https://github.com/Ferris-W/MSFormer

title: ParkOcc: A Novel Dataset and Benchmark for Surround-View Fisheye 3-D Semantic Occupancy Prediction in Automated Parking Scenarios
authors: Tianyu Yang, Yeqiang Qian, Chunxiang Wang, Ming Yang
abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction plays a vital role in fully understanding the surroundings, which has great potential in automated valet parking. Its comprehensive foreground and background awareness is well-suited for parking scenarios, which contain numerous background obstacles such as walls and pillars. During parking, the ego vehicle is often very close to these obstacles, requiring 3D fine-grained modeling of the surroundings. Therefore, considering that mass-produced vehicles are typically equipped with surround-view fisheye cameras, applying the occupancy prediction model based on fisheye cameras to parking perception is significant and promising. However, most existing works focus on applications in urban or highway scenarios, with insufficient attention given to parking scenarios. There are no available datasets or methods exploring the application of occupancy solutions in parking scenarios. To address this, we introduce a new surround-view fisheye occupancy dataset and benchmark called ParkOcc to promote research in dealing with diverse real-world parking cases. In addition, we also propose our new model, AdaptiveOcc v2, which utilizes joint forward and backward projection along with 2D and 3D auxiliary branches to achieve accurate performance. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness and exceptional generalizability of our approach. We hope the ParkOcc benchmark will boost the development of surrounding occupancy perception algorithms. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/yty-sky/ParkOcc

title: Lane-Changing Maneuver Prediction With Urban Arterial Traffic Data From Drones
authors: Sohyeong Kim, Pascal Frossard, Nikolas Geroliminis
abstract: This study addresses the challenge of predicting lane-change behavior in complex urban arterial environments, where interactions are heterogeneous and lane changing events are inherently rare. We propose Lane Change Direction and Timing Network (LC-DiTiNet), a Transformer-based framework that jointly predicts lane change direction and timing using an event-based formulation. To effectively handle the strong class imbalance between lane-keeping and lane changing events, we introduce a two-stage training strategy with focal loss, which stabilizes learning and improves performance on rare maneuvers. In addition, we propose a novel evaluation metric, the Driver Maneuver Prediction Index (DMPI), which integrates spatial (direction) and temporal (timing) accuracy through a normalized soft-DTW formulation, enabling a holistic assessment of maneuver prediction. Extensive experiments on drone-based urban traffic data demonstrate that the proposed model achieves robust performance across multiple prediction horizons, outperforming existing baselines particularly in long-horizon and minority-class scenarios. Furthermore, the model is computationally efficient, with approximately 2.02 million parameters and an inference time of 5.7 ms per vehicle, making it suitable for real-time intelligent transportation system (ITS) applications. These results highlight the effectiveness of jointly modeling maneuver direction and timing for capturing complex driver behavior in urban traffic.

title: Integrated Network Design and Demand Estimation for Advanced Air Mobility Using an Extended Multiple-Allocation p-Hub Median Framework
authors: Mahdi Monemi Nodehi, Yantong Dou, Joseph Post, Yu Zhang
abstract: It is essential to take the emerging transportation mode, Advanced Air Mobility (AAM), into transportation planning for developing a safe and efficient integrated multimodal transportation system. However, there are many operational uncertainties of AAM due to technological advancements, industry development, and regulatory establishment. Instead of operational details, e.g., fleet planning, eVTOL scheduling, and passenger assignment, transportation planners and policymakers want to know potential vertiport locations and the number and spatial distribution of travelers shifting from driving to using AAM services. To address these needs, our study examines the AAM integrated network design and demand estimation from a planning perspective. Given a traffic analysis zone (TAZ)-level origin and destination (OD) demand matrix, we propose an Extended Multiple Allocation p-Hub Median Problem (E-MApHMP) to determine optimal vertiport locations and estimate the shifted demand simultaneously. The objective of the mathematical programming is to minimize system-wide generalized travel cost, or, equivalently, to maximize the savings in generalized travel cost from shifting ground demand to air. A case study of Tampa Bay Region Plus (TBR+) involves 1,526 TAZs across seven counties, assuming each TAZ could potentially host one vertiport. Given the complexity of the problem, we developed a three-part chromosome-structured Genetic Algorithm (GA) with local search strategies to solve it efficiently. The traveler and socioeconomic data for this paper were drawn from a travel demand model developed for western Florida, US. Across multiple problem instances with fixed initial seeds, the proposed genetic algorithm (GA) consistently outperformed other metaheuristic algorithms and the Gurobi solver in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency. A factorial design sensitivity analysis was conducted to identify key parameters influencing AAM demand, the share of low-income travelers, and access and egress travel distances to vertiports. Results from the Type II ANOVA indicate that vertiport processing time, vertiport parking price, and the per-mile flying fee are the most significant factors affecting these outcomes.

title: Distributionally Robust Optimization for Location-Inventory-Allocation and Evacuation Planning Under Demand and Facility Disruption Uncertainties in Humanitarian Logistics
authors: Xueting Feng, Dujuan Wang, Yunqiang Yin, T. C. Edwin Cheng, Dunhu Liu
abstract: We investigate an integrated location-inventoryallocation and evacuation planning problem in disaster response, considering uncertainties in both the disruption ratios of distribution centers (DCs) and rescue shelters (RSs) and the demand of affected individuals for relief materials. Unlike conventional models that assume complete facility failures, our approach allows partially functional capacities at disrupted facilities. To capture these complexities, we develop a two-stage adaptive distributionally robust (TADR) optimization model. The first stage involves decisions regarding the locations of DCs, RSs, and backup warehouses (BWs), along with prepositioning inventory levels at DCs and BWs, prior to the realization of uncertain demand and facility disruption ratios. The second stage determines the allocation of relief materials from DCs and BWs to RSs and the evacuation planning for affected individuals from disaster areas to RSs, once these actual uncertainties are observed. To exactly solve the model, we reformulate it into a computationally tractable form and develop a customized Benders decomposition (BD) algorithm, incorporating two acceleration strategies to improve solution efficiency. The robustness and adaptability of our model and algorithm are validated through numerical experiments using randomly generated instances and realworld data from the Luding earthquake in China. The results demonstrate that: (i) The TADR model yields more reliable and flexible rescue plans compared to stochastic and deterministic benchmarks; (ii) The proposed algorithm achieves high computational efficiency; and (iii) Integrating BWs into the relief network plays a vital role in improving operational efficiency and reliability.

title: Accelerated Safety Evaluation for Autonomous Vehicles Using Markov Chain Score Ascent-Based Adaptive Importance Sampling
authors: Hao Wu, Yan Wu, Lifang Wang, Junzhi Zhang
abstract: Before autonomous vehicles are deployed on public roads at scale, it is crucial to quantify their safety. The failure probability of the autonomous vehicle is a key metric for evaluating their safety. However, the rarity of risk scenarios makes existing closed box-based failure probability estimation algorithms expensive. To address this issue, we propose Markov Chain Score Ascent-based Adaptive Importance Sampling (MCSA-AIS) to accelerate the safety evaluation of the autonomous vehicles. MCSA-AIS minimizes the inclusive KL divergence between a parameterized proposal distribution and the optimal importance sampling distribution from the perspective of stochastic gradient descent. Since the gradient of the inclusive KL divergence is defined as an expectation over the optimal importance sampling distribution to be approximated, an unbiased gradient estimate is required. To overcome this issue, MCSA-AIS utilizes the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to generate some test scenarios that follow the optimal importance sampling distribution, then estimates the unbiased gradients of the inclusive KL divergence and improves the proposal distribution. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, We take two autonomous driving systems as the System Under Test (SUT) and evaluate their failure probabilities in test scenarios. Experiments demonstrate that, compared with the baseline testing algorithms, the proposed method significantly improves the sample efficiency and accuracy of failure probability estimation.

title: Reinforcement Learning Approach for Traveling Salesman Problem With Drones in Dynamic Environment
authors: Qingwen Xue, Yu Jiang, Ye Yuan
abstract: The truck-drone collaborative systems in last-mile delivery can improve the flexibility and efficiency of logistics delivery, where the drones are not limited to the road traffic conditions. The Traveling Salesman Problem with Drones (TSP-D), which requires routing optimization of a heterogeneous fleet of vehicles in coordination, has become a vital problem to be solved. Most existing models tend to improve the delivery efficiency, considering the battery capacity and load limit of drones. In fact, the effect of dynamic environment is also important for TSP-D to be applicable in the real world. Therefore, the paper introduces additional challenges to traditional TSP, including truck-drone coordination, traffic variation and dynamic delivery demand, which complicate the optimization process and require robust and adaptive solution methods. We propose a Dynamic Reinforcement Learning for Truck-Drone Delivery (DRTDD) method integrating attention-based encoder-decoder to solve the TSP-D in dynamic environment. The state space of the DRTDD, encompassing vehicle status, dynamic demand information, and time-varying vehicle speeds, is updated at each time step, enabling the MDP to generate optimal routing decisions for both the truck and the drone. The method has been validated within the complex Shanghai freight transport network and real logistics dataset. This study offers an innovative method in the field of vehicle-drone coordinated routing optimization, with reinforcement learning to deal with traffic variation and dynamic delivery demand. It can help to establish a framework for future research on optimizing logistics and delivery systems in increasing complex and dynamic environment.

title: Act Natural! Naturalistic Projection for Traffic Analysis in Multimodal Behavior Scenarios
authors: Hamzah I. Khan, David Fridovich-Keil
abstract: Autonomous agents operating in traffic environments must consider how their behaviors might affect the human drivers around them, even when not directly interacting with them. To this end, it is often beneficial to be predictable and appear naturalistic. Existing methods for this purpose use human actor intent modeling or imitation learning techniques, but these approaches rarely capture all possible motivations for human behavior and/or require significant amounts of data. Our work extends a technique for modeling unimodal naturalistic behaviors with an explicit convex set representation, to account for multimodal behavior by using multiple convex sets. This more flexible representation provides a higher degree of fidelity in data-driven modeling of naturalistic behavior that arises in real-world scenarios in which human behavior is, in some sense, discrete, e.g. whether or not to yield at a roundabout. Equipped with this new set representation, we develop an optimization-based filter to project arbitrary trajectories into the set so that they appear naturalistic to humans in the scene, while also satisfying vehicle dynamics, actuator limits, etc. We demonstrate our methods on real-world human driving data from the inD (intersection) and rounD (roundabout) datasets.

title: Passenger Trajectory Model and Passenger Movement Estimation System for Preventing Passenger Subway Door Accidents
authors: Hee Jo, Yifan Li, Lisa Lim, Jo Woon Chong
abstract: Passengers being caught in subway doors can cause unexpected train delays and, in severe cases, serious injuries or loss of life. While previous studies have primarily focused on reactive methods that respond after passengers approach train doors, this study aims to proactively identify at-risk passengers before they reach the boarding area. We first develop a Passenger Trajectory Model (PTM) by analyzing the behavior of passengers descending stairs when a train is present at the station. Our analysis reveals that 97.85% of these passengers move directly toward the train doors, indicating that descending passengers are strong predictors of potential door-related incidents. Based on this behavioral insight, we propose a Passenger Movement Estimation System (PMES) that localizes passengers and classifies their movement types from single-frame Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) images. Three labeled datasets were constructed by annotating passengers into three movement classes: ascending, descending, and passing. The proposed PMES uses the YOLOv9 object detector for passenger localization and classification, while an ultra-lightweight custom architecture (SD-Net) enables efficient deployment. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves real-time performance with an mAP@0.5 of 97.58%. The framework is further validated across additional station environments with different layouts. Based on these results, we propose a Decision Support System (DSS) guideline to assist train operators in determining safe door-closing timing and suggest passenger-facing safety signage and alarm systems. The proposed framework can help reduce door-related accidents and minimize unexpected delays on subway platforms.

title: Self-Organizing Railway Traffic Management
authors: Federico Naldini, Fabio Oddi, Leo D’Amato, Grégory Marlière, Vito Trianni, Paola Pellegrini
abstract: Improving traffic management in case of perturbation is one of the main challenges in today's railway research. The great majority of the existing literature proposes approaches to make centralized decisions to minimize delay propagation. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm to the same aim: we design and implement a modular process to allow trains to self-organize. This process consists in having trains identifying their neighbors, formulating traffic management hypotheses, checking their compatibility and selecting the best ones through a consensus mechanism. Finally, these hypotheses are merged into a directly applicable traffic plan. In a thorough experimental analysis on a portion of the Italian network, we compare the results of self-organization with those of a state-of-the-art centralized approach. In particular, we make this comparison mimicking a realistic deployment thanks to a closed-loop framework including a microscopic railway simulator. The results indicate that self-organization achieves better results than the centralized algorithm, specifically thanks to the definition and exploitation of the instance decomposition allowed by the proposed approach.

title: Urban-Rural Bus-Assisted Drone Logistics Delivery With Time Window Considerations
authors: Yu Jiang, Chen Guo, Ye Yuan, Mengmeng Liu, Qingwen Xue
abstract: With the rapid growth of the e-commerce industry, the demand for parcel delivery in rural areas has been increasing year by year. However, long delivery distances and sparse population distribution make it difficult for traditional logistics providers to offer cost-effective services. To improve delivery efficiency by leveraging existing transport resources, this paper proposes a multi-visit bus-assisted drone routing problem considering customer points with soft time windows, called MV-BDRP-STW, which leverages urban-rural buses to assist drones in logistics distribution, combining the flexibility of drones with the accessibility of the bus system. The problem includes the following key components: 1) Multiple buses depart from the same station, each carrying a drone for logistics tasks, with drones launched and collected at bus stations; 2) Customer points are considered with soft time windows, and a penalty function is applied; and 3) Drones can serve multiple customer points in a single flight. We formulate the problem as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model and develop a two-stage heuristic algorithm to solve small- and large-scale instances with data based on real-world scenarios. The results validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and show significant cost reductions under different operational settings.

title: Virtual Coupled Train Set Intelligent Operation Control Method for High-Speed Railway Considering Carbon Emission Reduction
authors: Baiquan Tai, Zhi Zhang, Wencheng Huang
abstract: In this paper, we propose a virtual coupled train set intelligent operation control method for high-speed railway considering carbon emission reduction based on the Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework. Specifically, based on the theory of train dynamics, we consider the effects of slope, curvature, and tunnel conditions on the expected train spacing. Through analyzing the energy consumption of train operation, we take minimizing carbon emission reduction as one of the main control objectives and transform the virtual coupled train set intelligent operation control model into an optimal control problem. A real-world simulation experiment is conducted by using the Chengdu-Chongqing HSR as the background, we find that the model proposed in this paper performs effectively under line changing conditions, and can reduce a total of 0.72% of the traction carbon emissions of three follower trains. Finally, we compare the tracking errors and carbon emission reduction under three scenarios: different control objective weights (tracking and carbon emission), different time domains (predication and control), and different control strategies (moving block and virtual coupling). The results indicate that the proposed model requires a trade-off between tracking accuracy and carbon reduction effectiveness. To balance tracking precision and computational efficiency, it is recommended that the train’s horizon should not exceed 40. Compared to the moving block system, virtual coupling demonstrates outstanding advantages in terms of tracking interval and enhancing line capacity, and the proposed model can achieve a reduction of 2.81% in train traction carbon emissions.

title: Blockchain-Assisted Reliable Federated Learning in 5G-Powered Vehicular Systems
authors: Marcell Szabo, Laszlo Toka
abstract: The transformation of transport systems increasingly relies on connecting vehicles into cooperative networks, promising to reduce traffic congestion, lower emissions, and enhance road safety. Achieving these benefits requires efficient sharing of high definition (HD) map information across vehicles. Federated learning (FL) enables vehicles to collaboratively train shared models for HD maps, supporting accurate localization and dynamic environment understanding, without transferring raw data, thus preserving privacy. However, implementing FL in this context faces significant challenges: malicious participants can disrupt learning, and honest participants may disengage without sufficient incentives. To address these issues, we propose integrating a dual blockchain framework with FL, which evaluates participant reliability, weights contributions accordingly, and provides financial incentives to maintain engagement. This coordinated approach ensures that only trustworthy information contributes to HD map updates, preserving both data privacy and system integrity. By modeling and optimizing the system’s economic utility, and validating through simulations, we demonstrate that the framework is feasible under realistic settings when reward and subscription fees are appropriately calibrated, providing a robust foundation for secure, incentivized, and privacy preserving vehicular networks.
